Thermodynamics

 Home Physics Branches of physics Statistical physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 80k Articles: 678
Thermodynamics studies energy transfers and the constraints on macroscopic changes. Its vocabulary connects internal energy, entropy, temperature, pressure and volume to heat and work. The first law of thermodynamics balances energy; the Second law of thermodynamics decides which changes can occur spontaneously and limits how much work a heat engine can deliver. These principles let us bound performance before choosing a material or a detailed machine design. Applications include power generation, propulsion and refrigerators. [ref]
Start by choosing a system boundary. A closed system can exchange energy but no matter; an isolated system exchanges neither. A state function, such as internal energy or entropy, depends on the equilibrium state. A process specifies how that state changes. Thus a body's temperature is a property it has, whereas heat records energy crossing its boundary during a process. A body contains internal energy, rather than a stored quantity of heat.
Two insulated bodies initially at different positive temperatures approach thermal equilibrium when brought into thermal contact. Their combined energy is conserved, but their combined entropy increases. They do not spontaneously separate again into a hotter body and a colder one. This familiar asymmetry makes thermodynamics interesting: conserving energy leaves many imaginable changes available, and entropy supplies a further constraint. The same distinction underlies both entropy maximization under thermal contact and the thermal efficiency limit in Carnot's theorem.

State of matter

Words: 917 Articles: 25
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A state of matter is a broad category of material behavior. A solid resists a sustained change of shape, a liquid flows while remaining difficult to compress, and a gas expands to fill its container. These distinctions are useful first descriptions, but they do not enumerate all thermodynamic phases. Plasma adds collective behavior of charged particles, while liquid crystals show that flow and structural order need not disappear together.
Distinguish three questions: what broad state of matter does the material resemble, which thermodynamic phase is present, and what are its temperature, pressure and other state variables? Two samples at different temperatures can be in the same liquid thermodynamic phase. Conversely, crystal polymorphism gives different solid thermodynamic phases of the same substance, distinguished by their crystal structures. A phase transition between them need not change the broad state-of-matter category.
For an imagined substance with crystalline forms A and B, melting A produces a solid–liquid phase transition, while converting A to B produces a solid–solid phase transition. A sample containing A and B has two thermodynamic phases even though all its material is solid. Cutting one uniform crystal into two pieces does not create a second thermodynamic phase: count distinct equilibrium forms, rather than pieces or grains. This distinction matters when applying the phase rule.
A phase diagram locates stable thermodynamic phases using temperature and pressure. Its liquid–gas phase coexistence curve ends at a liquid-gas critical point, around which a path connects liquid and gas without a first-order phase transition. Broad categories can therefore remain useful without a sharp boundary.[ref]

Thermodynamic equilibrium

Words: 515 Articles: 5
Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
A thermodynamic system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when its macroscopic state has no spontaneous tendency to change through any exchange allowed by its constraints. For an isolated system, stable thermodynamic equilibrium maximizes entropy over the accessible states at fixed total energy and conserved material inventories. A wall can forbid an exchange, so always specify what can cross or move. Thermal, mechanical and chemical conditions answer different questions about that same constrained state. [ref]
For example, two compartments separated by a rigid, impermeable wall that transmits heat can reach thermal equilibrium while retaining different pressures and compositions. Allowing an unloaded piston to move adds a mechanical equilibrium condition. Allowing one chemical species to cross adds chemical potential equality for particle exchange; allowing a chemical reaction adds its chemical equilibrium condition. A fixed barrier can therefore support a constrained thermodynamic equilibrium that ceases to be an equilibrium when the barrier is removed.
Uniformity is not the definition of thermodynamic equilibrium. An isothermal atmosphere in hydrostatic equilibrium can have a common temperature while its pressure and mass density vary with height: the pressure gradient balances gravity. In an external field, the exchange condition must include the relevant potential energy; for charged matter this leads to the electrochemical potential. Relativistic gravitational corrections to thermal equilibrium are described separately by the Tolman temperature law.
A steady state only says that the macroscopic description is constant in time. A bar maintained between hot and cold thermal reservoirs has steady heat flux and produces entropy, so it is not in thermodynamic equilibrium. Even matching temperatures at one perfect-contact interface can coexist with heat transfer through the surrounding material; matching those two local values does not establish equilibrium of the whole apparatus. See thermal conduction for that spatial transport problem.
The useful simplification is that equilibrium conditions predict an endpoint without computing every collision or flow during relaxation. The first law of thermodynamics supplies the conserved quantities, and the Second law of thermodynamics supplies the direction of change. For a system held at fixed temperature and volume, the corresponding criterion is minimization of Helmholtz free energy; at fixed temperature and pressure, it is minimization of Gibbs free energy, with the material and exchange constraints still imposed.

Mechanical balance is also needed; interface curvature can require a pressure jump rather than equal bulk pressures.

Mechanical equilibrium requires force balance for the mechanical displacements that are allowed. Two uniform fluids separated by a freely moving, unloaded, frictionless piston with equal face areas require equal pressures. A supported piston can sustain a pressure difference, and a fluid in gravity instead obeys hydrostatic equilibrium. For an upward height coordinate z, that balance is dp/dz=−ρg, where ρ is mass density and g is the downward gravitational acceleration. Mechanical equilibrium alone does not establish thermal equilibrium or chemical equilibrium.

Thermodynamic stability OurBigBook.com
For a mechanical coordinate x at fixed temperature, total volume and particle numbers, the relevant thermodynamic potential is the Helmholtz free energy F(x). Its generalized force is f=−F′(x). At mechanical equilibrium, f(x∗​)=0, and a linearly restoring force has f′(x∗​)<0, equivalently F′′(x∗​)>0. A Taylor expansion then proves a strict local free-energy minimum. If F is a strictly convex function throughout the accessible domain, the stationary state is the unique global minimum.

Closed system

Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
A closed system exchanges no matter with its surroundings, but can exchange energy through heat or work. A sealed cylinder with a moving piston is a typical idealized example. “Closed” fixes the material inventory, rather than the volume or the internal energy. An insulated cylinder can receive compression work; a rigid sealed vessel can receive heat. Neither is necessarily an isolated system.

Isolated system

Words: 103
Thermodynamic system OurBigBook.com
An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings. Its total energy is fixed, while the Second law of thermodynamics requires its total entropy to be nondecreasing. Its internal energy alone is fixed when bulk kinetic energy and external potential energy also remain unchanged. For example, an initially spinning stirrer inside an insulated rigid vessel can lose kinetic energy while the contents gain internal energy, with no external input.
An isolated system need not yet be in thermodynamic equilibrium. Two enclosed bodies at different temperatures can exchange heat internally until they reach thermal equilibrium; their combined energy stays constant. Their internal transfer is absent from the outer boundary ledger. A vacuum-insulated container is only an approximation to isolation: residual thermal conduction and thermal radiation can still carry energy across its boundary.

Quasistatic process

Words: 899
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A quasistatic process is an ideal limit in which a changing thermodynamic system passes through a sequence of states arbitrarily close to thermodynamic equilibrium. Its intermediate pressure, temperature and volume are therefore well defined and obey its equation of state. Driving must be slow compared with the system's own equilibration, rather than merely taking a long time on a clock. A reversible thermodynamic process additionally allows both system and surroundings to be restored without net change; friction can produce entropy even in a quasistatic process.[ref]
For a computed example, take a fixed amount of substance n of ideal gas in a sealed cylinder with a frictionless piston, in contact with a heat bath at absolute temperature T. Reduce the external load in infinitesimal steps so that the piston expands from V0​ to 2V0​. In the reversible limit, the gas pressure exceeds the external pressure by an infinitesimal amount during expansion, and the heat transfer occurs across an infinitesimal temperature difference. Exact mechanical equilibrium would give no driving force; the limiting imbalance supplies motion while preserving equilibrium intermediate states.[ref]
Along this reversible isothermal expansion, the ideal gas law gives
p(V)=VnRT​,nRT=1kJ,V0​=1L=10−3m3,p0​=V0​nRT​=1MPa.
(1)
Here R is the molar gas constant; specifying nRT fixes an energy scale, without choosing n and T separately. The initial and final equilibrium states are (V0​,p0​,T) and (2V0​,p0​/2,T). Count work delivered to the surroundings as positive. The reversible work is the shaded area beneath the pressure-volume curve:
Wout,rev​=∫V0​2V0​​p(V)dV=nRTln2≈0.693147kJ.
(2)
The integral of 1/V supplies the natural logarithm. Since internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, ΔU=0; the first law of thermodynamics, ΔU=Qin​−Wout​, gives Qin,rev​=0.693147kJ to the displayed precision. The heat bath replaces the energy delivered as work.[ref]
Now start from the same initial state, but abruptly lower the external pressure to the constant value pext​=p0​/2=0.5MPa. There is a finite initial pressure imbalance, so this is an irreversible expansion rather than a quasistatic process. Assume the piston begins and ends at rest, has no net change in stored energy, and has no external friction; relaxation occurs within the gas and its heat bath. After motion has settled and the heat bath has restored temperature T, mechanical equilibrium and the ideal gas law give Vf​=nRT/pext​=2V0​. The work delivered to the constant load is
Wout,load​=pext​(Vf​−V0​)=(0.5MPa)(1L)=0.5kJ,ΔU=0,Qin,load​=0.5kJ.
(3)
This work follows directly from load force times piston displacement, using dV=Adx for piston area A. Intermediate gas states need not have a single equilibrium pressure or temperature. In particular, neither p(V)=nRT/V at the bath temperature nor p(V)=pext​ describes the actual gas during this irreversible motion. The rectangle below plots the known external load; its upper edge is not an equilibrium gas path.
The entropy accounting makes the difference precise. Because entropy is a state function, both expansions have the same gas entropy change, computed along the reversible isothermal expansion:
ΔSgas​=∫V0​2V0​​TδQrev​​=nRln2.
(4)
The thermal reservoir stays at T and loses heat Qin​=Wout​, so ΔSbath​=−Wout​/T. Assume the ideal load stores work without an entropy change. The combined entropy production is therefore
ΔStotal​=nRln2−TWout​​={0,nR(ln2−1/2)>0,​reversible expansion,constant external load.​
(5)
No numerical entropy unit is implied by nRT=1kJ alone: nR or T must also be specified. The lost work opportunity is TΔStotal​=0.193147kJ for this comparison. This calculation uses equilibrium endpoints and the reservoir's temperature, without assigning equilibrium intermediate states to the irreversible gas. [ref]
For another boundary choice, let the same ideal gas expand into an initially evacuated compartment of volume V0​ inside a rigid, insulated vessel of total volume 2V0​. Removing the partition causes free expansion: no load is moved and no heat crosses the outer boundary, so Wout​=Qin​=0 and ΔU=0. After equilibration the temperature is again T, the pressure is p0​/2, and the gas entropy has increased by nRln2. The outer vessel has fixed volume; the gas's accessible volume doubles. Restoring the initial gas state requires compression and removal of heat, changing the surroundings. Equal endpoints do not make free expansion reversible. [ref]
A slowly moving piston with dry friction supplies a different caution: its gas can remain arbitrarily close to thermodynamic equilibrium, yet rubbing still converts work into heat and produces entropy. If the frictional force has a nonzero slow-motion limit, its dissipated energy over a fixed travel does not vanish with speed. Reversing the motion reverses friction, so infinitesimally changing the external load cannot retrace the same operation and restore the surroundings. The heat capacity calculations additionally exclude friction and other dissipative work.[ref]
The usefulness of a quasistatic process is that it replaces detailed motion by a readable sequence of equilibrium states. An equation of state and an integral then turn a pressure-volume drawing into an energy budget. The beautiful distinction is that internal energy and entropy depend on the endpoints, while heat and work record how the change was performed. Reversible benchmarks expose how much work an irreversible device sacrifices, while entropy production explains why simply making it slower need not recover that opportunity.

State function

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A state function assigns a value to each equilibrium thermodynamic state of a specified thermodynamic system. Its change depends only on the initial and final states. Internal energy U, entropy S and enthalpy H=U+pV are state functions; here p is pressure and V is volume. Transferred heat Q and work W belong to a thermodynamic process, rather than to a state. A system stores internal energy; it does not store separate inventories of “heat received” and “work received”.[ref]
Use the explicit convention Q>0 for heat entering and Wby​>0 for work done by the thermodynamic system on its surroundings. For a closed system with unchanged endpoint bulk kinetic energy and external potential energy, the first law of thermodynamics reads
ΔU=Q−Wby​,dU=δQ−δWby​.
(6)
The notation dU denotes an exact differential of a state function; δQ and δWby​ denote incremental transfers. Along a reversible thermodynamic process of a simple compressible system,
δWby,rev​=pdV,δQrev​=TdS,
(7)
where T is absolute temperature. These are rules for particular thermodynamic processes, not definitions of stored heat or stored work. In particular, a quasistatic process with friction can remain near thermodynamic equilibrium while producing entropy.[ref]
For any state function F and two equilibrium states A,B, an integral of its exact differential gives
∫AB​dF=F(B)−F(A),∮dF=0.
(8)
The proof is telescoping: add the changes F(xi+1​)−F(xi​) along a subdivided path, and all intermediate values cancel. The smooth limit gives the integral. Conversely, if an integrable differential form has zero integral around every accessible closed path in a connected region, define F(B) by integrating from a reference state. Two routes differ by a closed path, so the definition is unambiguous. This argument needs every accessible loop, rather than a local test that might miss a hole in the domain; see path independence.
The same cancellation does not hold separately for heat and work. A thermodynamic cycle has ΔU=0 but can have nonzero net transfers, with ∮δQ=∮δWby​. Nor does the fact that entropy is a state function make Q/T its general change: the formula dS=δQrev​/T uses a reversible thermodynamic process and its varying temperature.
This distinction makes endpoint calculations powerful. We can compute an internal energy, entropy or enthalpy difference along a convenient reversible reference path even when the actual thermodynamic process is irreversible. Its actual heat and work must still be obtained from its own boundary interactions. The appealing cancellation is visible in two reversible ideal-gas paths between the same states: a different mechanical output requires a matching difference in thermal input, while stored internal energy arrives at the same value.

Two reversible ideal-gas paths between the same states

State function OurBigBook.com
Take a closed system consisting of one mole of a classical monatomic gas, idealized as an ideal gas with constant heat capacity at constant volume CV​=3nR/2. Stipulate amount of substance n=1mol and molar gas constant R=8.314Jmol−1K−1 for this calculation. Set initial temperature T0​=300K and volume V0​=0.010m3, and define E0​=nRT0​=2.4942kJ and p0​=E0​/V0​=249.42kPa. The specified equilibrium endpoints are
A:(V,T,p)=(V0​,T0​,p0​),B:(V,T,p)=(3V0​,2T0​,2p0​/3).
(9)
Thus B has volume 0.030m3, temperature 600K and pressure 166.28kPa. The fixed material inventory and ideal gas law make these complete endpoint specifications for this model. All numbers below are calculated values, rather than measurements of a particular gas.
Use a frictionless piston, ignore bulk mechanical energy changes, and allow only pressure-volume work. Each step is the limit of a reversible thermodynamic process: adjust loads by infinitesimal pressure differences, and supply heat through infinitesimal temperature differences. Heating with changing temperature requires a succession of matching thermal reservoirs; contact with a single hotter heat bath would give an irreversible finite difference. On a fixed-volume leg the piston is locked. These assumptions justify using the actual equilibrium path's pressure in
Wby,rev​=∫path​pdV.
(10)
An endpoint chord is not the path; substituting a guessed straight line would compute a different thermodynamic process.[ref]
The upper route heats at fixed volume from A to C=(V0​,2T0​,2p0​), then undergoes isothermal expansion at 2T0​ to B. The lower route undergoes isothermal expansion at T0​ from A to D=(3V0​,T0​,p0​/3), then heats at fixed volume to B. The tuples use the same (V,T,p) ordering as the endpoints. Vertical legs do zero expansion work, and the two curved legs have different pressures at every shared intermediate volume.
The internal energy of an ideal gas gives the same endpoint difference for both routes:
ΔU=23​nR(2T0​−T0​)=23​E0​=3.7413kJ.
(11)
On either fixed-volume heating leg, Wby​=0 and Q=3E0​/2. On each isothermal expansion, ΔU=0, so the first law of thermodynamics gives Q=Wby​. The ideal gas law and the integral of 1/V then give
Wby,upper​Wby,lower​​=∫V0​3V0​​V2E0​​dV=2E0​ln3,=∫V0​3V0​​VE0​​dV=E0​ln3,​Qupper​Qlower​​=23​E0​+2E0​ln3,=23​E0​+E0​ln3.​
(12)
Here ln is the natural logarithm. Rounded to 0.001kJ, the upper route has (Q,Wby​,ΔU)=(9.222,5.480,3.741)kJ and the lower route has (6.481,2.740,3.741)kJ. Subtracting separately rounded entries can differ by 0.001kJ; the unrounded balances are exact in the stipulated model.
The shaded area between the curves explains the entire difference:

Following the upper route forward and the lower route backward makes a thermodynamic cycle with this positive net work and matching net heat. Its internal energy change is zero. The two open routes themselves are reversible, so their different work outputs should not be mistaken for a loss caused by entropy production: they receive different heat transfers at different temperatures.
Two other state functions provide independent endpoint checks. With enthalpy H=5nRT/2 in this model,
ΔH=25​E0​=6.2355kJ,ΔS=23​nRln2+nRln3≈17.7781JK−1.

To obtain the entropy change along either route, integrate CV​dT/T on its heating leg, giving CV​ln2, and nRdV/V on its isothermal expansion, giving nRln3. Reordering the legs changes their heat totals but leaves the sum of their entropy changes unchanged. In particular, neither route's total Q divided by its final temperature equals ΔS, and neither total Q equals ΔH: both routes include an isothermal expansion, rather than a single fixed-pressure heating step.

Heat engine

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A heat engine uses a repeating thermodynamic cycle to turn part of an incoming heat transfer into net outgoing work. In the two-thermal reservoir model, the hot thermal reservoir supplies heat Qh​>0 at fixed temperature Th​, and the cold thermal reservoir receives heat of magnitude Qc​>0 at fixed temperature Tc​<Th​. A Stirling engine makes the repeated motion visible; the abstract energy budget applies independently of its particular mechanism.[ref]
Choose the entire cyclic device as a closed system, with no net change in bulk kinetic energy or potential energy. Count heat entering as positive and net work delivered as positive, as in the first law of thermodynamics. Thus Qh​ enters with a plus sign and Qc​, although a positive magnitude, enters with a minus sign. Assume these two heat transfers and the net work are the only transfers across the boundary. Over one complete thermodynamic cycle, all stored energy, including internal energy U, returns to its starting value:
ΔU=Qh​−Qc​−W=0,W=Qh​−Qc​.
(16)
The device does not accumulate heat from cycle to cycle. More precisely, heat is a transfer, while internal energy is what can be stored; even a component that temporarily stores internal energy must return to its initial state for this boundary to be cyclic.[ref]
For engine operation, Qh​>Qc​ and W>0. Its thermal efficiency is
η=Qh​W​=1−Qh​Qc​​.
(17)
Use net work, after subtracting any work supplied during compression or required by auxiliaries included in the chosen device. For periodic operation, average power satisfies Pout​=Q˙​h​−Q˙​c​ and η=Pout​/Q˙​h​, with the rates averaged over complete thermodynamic cycles.[ref]
For a stipulated model at Th​=600K and Tc​=300K, let Qh​=1000J and Qc​=600J per thermodynamic cycle. Then W=400J and η=2/5=40%. At two thermodynamic cycles per second, these become 2000W incoming heat transfer, 1200W outgoing heat transfer, and 800W net power. These are constructed values, not measurements.
Different signs describe different tasks. With the same directions of heat transfer, Qh​=Qc​ gives W=0: a device transmitting heat without net work output. If Qc​>Qh​, net work is supplied to that device. A refrigerator or heat pump instead extracts heat from the cold side and delivers heat to the hot side, using positive input work Win​ and the balance Qh​=Qc​+Win​. Their useful output is heat transfer, measured by a coefficient of performance. Finally, a one-time isothermal expansion can have Q=W and ΔU=0 while leaving the volume changed: it is not a complete thermodynamic cycle. A warming device also fails the cyclic assumption, and a fuel-consuming device requires an accounting of matter crossing its boundary.
For two fixed thermal reservoirs at positive thermodynamic temperatures, the Second law of thermodynamics strengthens the energy balance to
η≤ηC​=1−Th​Tc​​.
(18)
Equality requires the overall operation to be a reversible thermodynamic process, including its heat transfer to the thermal reservoirs. The Carnot cycle explains how the reversible benchmark is constructed, and Carnot's theorem explains its universality and the entropy production penalty. Use kelvin values, never ratios of degree Celsius readings. The example above lies below the 50% bound: its total entropy production is −1000/600+600/300=1/3JK−1 per thermodynamic cycle.
This is useful before building a machine: warmer cooling surroundings reduce the possible thermal efficiency, even if the mechanism is unchanged. A small observed thermal efficiency does not by itself test the Second law of thermodynamics; heat leaks, friction, incomplete recovery of work, and the measurement boundary can all reduce the reported ratio. A meaningful comparison requires the actual thermal reservoir temperatures, matched heat and net work measurements, and the hypotheses of Carnot's theorem. Finite bodies whose temperatures change are treated separately there.
The practical question already appears in the 1824 Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu et sur les machines propres à développer cette puissance by Sadi Carnot: pp. 6–8 ask whether machines driven by heat have a fundamental limit and whether changing the working substance can improve their output. Pages 9–11 describe heating and cooling in real machines, but use the historical caloric theory, rather than the modern first law of thermodynamics balance. The historical discussion under Carnot's theorem explains that distinction.

A Stirling engine repeatedly heats and cools a confined gas, whose expansion and compression drive a moving mechanical load. This makes it a particularly accessible example of a heat engine: both the repeating motion and the two regions exchanging heat can be observed.
In the published Demonstration experiments with a Stirling engine by Christopher G Deacon and others, an electrical heater warms one end of a cylinder and flowing water cools the other at 12∘C. A moving displacer shuttles gas through copper wool that temporarily stores and returns internal energy. A laser spot traces a closed pressure-volume path on a screen: mechanical motion controls one coordinate, pressure the other. Calibrating both scales converts the enclosed area to work per thermodynamic cycle; multiplying by rotation frequency gives gas-cycle power. At 97W heater input, the paper reports 4.4W gas-cycle power, while a separate Prony brake measures 3.4W shaft output. The cold-side temperature is controlled and two higher heater settings are compared. The gas has a nonuniform temperature, and heater energy also escapes to the room: neither output/input ratio measures W/Qh​ for an ideal two-thermal reservoir engine. These observations demonstrate work production and losses, not a direct measurement of the bound in Carnot's theorem. The inspected apparatus, readouts and results are on pp. 180–182, Figures 1–3 and Table 1.

Refrigerator

Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A refrigerator removes heat from the region we want to keep cold and releases heat to warmer surroundings. Here we consider a work-driven cyclic device: its useful output is the cold-side extraction Qc​, and its input is net work W. A food compartment is a familiar example; the same cooling objective applies when removing heat from a room. The coefficient of performance measures extraction per unit work, rather than the fraction of input energy converted into output. [ref]
Choose the complete machine as the thermodynamic system. Let Qc​>0 be heat entering from the colder side, Qh​>0 be heat delivered to the hotter side, and W>0 be net work supplied, all over the same complete cycle. Assume these are its only energy transfers, no matter crosses the outer boundary, and there is no net change in stored energy. Returning to the initial state gives ΔU=0, so the first law of thermodynamics reads
0=Qc​−Qh​+W,Qh​=Qc​+W.
(20)
The heat leaving the warmer side includes both the extracted heat and the supplied work. For instance, stipulated transfers Qc​=3kJ and W=1kJ require Qh​=4kJ; the cooling coefficient of performance is 3. This is an illustrative budget, not measured performance. At steady operation the same balance holds for average transfer rates, Q˙​h​=Q˙​c​+Pin​, where Pin​ is input power.
This budget explains a useful counterexample: operating a refrigerator with its door open inside an otherwise isolated room cannot cool the room as a whole. If both heat transfers occur within the room and the electrical input comes from outside, the room gains Qh​−Qc​=W each cycle. Locally cold air does not imply net cooling. The Second law of thermodynamics permits cold-to-hot transfer because work is supplied; it forbids a cyclic device whose sole effect is that transfer. See the Clausius statement of the second law.

Vapor-compression refrigeration circulates a working fluid through cold and hot coils. In the cold coil, liquid becomes gas while absorbing heat from the refrigerated region. Compression supplies work and raises the pressure and temperature; the hot coil releases heat as the gas returns to liquid. A restriction reduces the pressure before the next cold-side passage. Changing the pressure changes the temperature of the phase transition, letting one circulating fluid receive and release heat at different temperatures. This physical implementation serves both refrigerators and heat pumps; its ordinary dissipative operation differs from the reversible Carnot cycle used to bound performance. [ref] [ref]

A heat pump uses work to deliver heat to the region we want to keep warm. Its useful output is the hot-side delivery Qh​. The same operating machine can be described as a refrigerator when the cold-side extraction Qc​ is the objective: which output is useful changes the coefficient of performance, while the energy balance stays Qh​=Qc​+W. Heating a water bath by taking heat from a colder water bath makes this distinction visible in the heat-pump calorimetry experiment below. [ref]
In the illustrative budget from refrigerator, supplying 1kJ of work delivers 4kJ of useful heat, giving a heating coefficient of performance of 4. The additional 3kJ came from the colder region. Compare an ideal electrical heater whose entire input work becomes heat in the target region: it delivers 1kJ for that input. The appeal of a heat pump is this ability to move existing energy, while the Second law of thermodynamics limits the work saving for a given pair of temperatures.

One bath cooling while the other warms makes the origin of the delivered energy observable. [ref]
The following analysis extends that procedure to simultaneous measurements of both finite baths. Weigh the water in each vessel; determine the effective heat capacities Cc​ and Ch​, including immersed hardware, by a separate known electrical-input calibration over the working temperature range. A matched pair of calibrated thermometers placed in stirred water measures bulk Tc​(t) and Th​(t); keeping probes away from the coils avoids mistaking a local contact temperature for the whole bath. Record the room temperature and synchronise the electrical meter and thermometry. Use short intervals after startup, with no boiling or freezing and small enough temperature changes that constant effective heat capacities are a reasonable approximation. Over a common interval [t0​,t1​], the uncorrected bath estimates and measured electrical input are

Writing Lh​>0 for outward hot-bath leak power and Lc​>0 for inward cold-bath leak power, the bath balances give

Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Free expansion occurs when a gas spreads into an initially evacuated region without driving an external load. The standard idealization uses a rigid, insulated vessel: initially a partition confines the gas to volume V1​, while the remaining compartment contains vacuum. Open a passage and wait for thermodynamic equilibrium; the same fixed amount of substance n now occupies the larger accessible volume V2​. The outer vessel never changes size. This simple release separates three questions: what energy is conserved, whether temperature changes, and why entropy increases. [ref]
Choose the gas as the closed system, neglect heat exchange with the walls, and assume negligible changes in bulk kinetic energy and potential energy between the equilibrium endpoints. Insulation gives Qin​=0; no moving outer boundary or external load receives work, so Wout​=0. The first law of thermodynamics therefore gives
ΔU=Qin​−Wout​=0.
(28)
The gas can develop internal motion during the release; this does not supply external work. The intermediate state need not have one equilibrium pressure or temperature, so there is no actual quasistatic process curve p(V) to integrate. In particular, substituting the equilibrium ideal gas law into ∫pdV would describe a different process. [ref]
For an ideal gas, internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. With positive heat capacity at constant volume, U(T2​)=U(T1​) implies T2​=T1​, and the ideal gas law gives p2​/p1​=V1​/V2​. Doubling the accessible volume thus halves the final pressure without changing the final temperature. This is an endpoint statement; it does not assert a spatially uniform, constant temperature during the rush. Insulation alone does not imply constant temperature: a reversible adiabatic expansion cools an ideal gas because it supplies work. [ref]
For a real gas, U(T,V) can depend on volume as well as temperature, so unchanged internal energy need not mean unchanged temperature. For a fixed-composition simple compressible system in a single thermodynamic phase, equilibrium identities using a Maxwell relation give
dU=CV​dT+[T(∂T∂p​)V​−p]dV,(∂V∂T​)U​=CV​p−T(∂p/∂T)V​​.
(29)
Here CV​ is the whole sample's heat capacity at constant volume. The sign depends on the equation of state; for an ideal gas the numerator vanishes. For a finite free expansion, solve U(T2​,V2​)=U(T1​,V1​), or integrate this slope along equilibrium states of equal internal energy; that mathematical curve does not describe the actual release. [ref]
Free expansion is useful because it tests how internal energy depends on number density while eliminating external expansion work. Its beautiful surprise is that an ideal gas can finish with the same temperature and internal energy but greater entropy: a thermometer alone cannot diagnose reversibility. See entropy change in free expansion for the calculation and temperature sensitivity of a free-expansion experiment for the experimental qualification. The continuous-flow throttling associated with the Joule-Thomson coefficient has a different balance: under its usual assumptions it preserves enthalpy, whereas the gas-only idealization here preserves internal energy. In his paper published in 1845, Joule connected two copper receivers with stopcocks, filled one with compressed dry air, and evacuated the other with an air pump. He immersed the connected receivers in water in an insulated arrangement, stirred the water, and read a sensitive thermometer. He then opened the stopcocks, let the air redistribute, stirred again, and compared the water's temperature with its initial value. Alternating control trials accounted for effects such as stirring and evaporation. The observation was no detectable net cooling of the common bath, rather than a record of the gas temperature at every instant. [ref] [ref]
Joule also immersed the receivers and their connecting piece in separate water vessels. The source receiver cooled while the receiving side warmed, with nearly cancelling thermal effects. [ref]
This distinguishes local transient changes from the final observation for the combined apparatus. Insulating its outer boundary suppresses external heat exchange; it does not prevent heat exchange between the gas, the receivers and the water inside that boundary.
An idealized modern version can use two rigid chambers joined by a valve, with thermometers in the chambers and on the walls. Prepare one chamber with gas and the other evacuated, disconnect the pump, close the apparatus to matter exchange, and let the initial temperature settle. Record initial and final equilibrium pressure and temperature, along with the wall response. Repeated closed-valve runs can reveal drift and valve-actuation effects; independent heating calibrations can estimate the heat capacity of the participating apparatus. This is a proposed measurement protocol, not a claim of a particular measured result. Fast local readings can characterize the release, but they cannot replace the final equilibrium readings in the endpoint internal energy balance.

Zeroth law of thermodynamics

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Laws of thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
If two thermodynamic systems are each in thermal equilibrium with the same third system in the same equilibrium state, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Write A∼B for this relation. The zeroth law of thermodynamics supplies transitivity:
A∼CandB∼C⟹A∼B.
(33)
Its symmetric relation property and self-equilibrium (reflexivity), together with transitivity, make thermal equilibrium an equivalence relation. Its equivalence classes can be labelled by a common empirical temperature; choosing an absolute numerical scale requires the further structure of thermodynamic temperature.[ref]
The comparison assumes internally equilibrated macroscopic bodies, unchanged composition and mechanical constraints, and contact permitting only heat exchange. Use rigid, impermeable diathermal walls so that neither matter transfer nor boundary work spoils the test. The same state of C matters: letting C warm while measuring A, then cool while measuring B, does not supply the premise. Ordinary nonrelativistic laboratory thermodynamics is assumed; the Tolman temperature law treats gravitational qualifications. Equal temperatures establish the thermal condition, without requiring mechanical equilibrium or chemical equilibrium.
This explains why a thermometer can compare unlike materials: it supplies a reusable third system. A temperature is a property of an equilibrium state, while heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Two bodies at the same temperature can have different internal energies and heat capacities. A thermometer therefore does not measure a body's stored amount of heat; the finite-body disturbance and waiting-time calculations in thermometer describe how making the comparison can change the state being measured.[ref]
The name “zeroth” reflects logical order rather than the date of the first thermometer: this premise about thermal equilibrium precedes the already numbered first law of thermodynamics, Second law of thermodynamics and third law of thermodynamics. This is the naming explanation given in University Physics Volume 2 by Samuel J. Ling and others (§1.1, “Thermal Equilibrium”).[ref]
The corresponding Zeroth law of black-hole mechanics states constancy of surface gravity over an equilibrium horizon; Hawking radiation identifies that quantity with physical temperature up to its universal conversion factor.

If XA​=XB​, and the calibrated response is an injective function of temperature on this range, C occupies the same thermal reference state in both comparisons. Thus equal 37mm readings in separately equilibrated samples test equal temperatures, regardless of how much internal energy those samples contain. Reference-bath thermometer comparison
Words: 291
Zeroth-law thermometer comparison OurBigBook.com
A motivating real procedure is NIST's ambient thermometer verification. Its apparatus is a deep beaker of water, a calibrated reference thermometer, a test thermometer, and a magnetic stirrer with any heater switched off. Let the water approach room temperature, stir gently, immerse both sensing tips well below the surface, and wait before reading. NIST specifies about 20cm of water, 10–15cm immersion where possible, and an initial five-minute wait. Record test then reference, repeat in reverse order, and apply the reference's certificate correction. Subtract corrected reference from test: the difference estimates the test instrument's error at this bath temperature. Agreement between the two reading orders checks repeatability. [ref]
For example, suppose a test reads 24.7∘C, a reference reads 24.4∘C, and its certificate says to add 0.1∘C. The corrected reference is 24.5∘C, so the test error is +0.2∘C: it reads high. These are illustrative readings. This verification tests a previously calibrated instrument at one point; it does not establish the two-point response used in two-point thermometer calibration example.
Additional controls follow from the thermal equilibrium premise. Keep tips away from walls and bottom, interchange probe positions to test a temperature gradient, and check that longer waits and modest immersion changes leave agreement unchanged within the required tolerance. A flat trace alone can be a steady state maintained by competing heat transfer paths. Five minutes is a procedural starting point, not a universal equilibration time. Excessive stirring can supply work and warm the bath, while probe stems can exchange heat with the room. These controls test whether both probes sample the same state; neither one-point agreement nor this experiment proves the zeroth law of thermodynamics for every material and condition.

Diffusion is net transport associated with random microscopic motion. A localized patch of a dilute solute can spread through a stationary solvent: individual molecules move in both directions, but more cross from the crowded side of an imaginary surface than from the less crowded side. This imbalance gives a net diffusive flux down the concentration gradient; the molecules do not need to sense which direction has lower concentration. At uniform concentration, microscopic exchanges continue even though the net diffusive flux vanishes. [ref]
The distinction from advection is easiest to see in a dye patch. Uniform bulk motion carries its centre downstream; diffusion broadens it relative to that centre. Both can happen together. A moving or spreading patch by itself does not identify the mechanism: a nonuniform velocity field can also stretch a patch. [ref]
For a dilute nonreacting solute in a uniform medium at fixed temperature, Fick's first law models the relative diffusive flux as j=−D∇C, with scalar diffusion coefficient D>0 of units m2s−1. Here C is the amount of substance per unit volume, so j has units molm−2s−1. With carrier velocity field u, the total flux is Cu+j. The continuity equation, with no sources or chemical reactions, gives
∂t∂C​+∇⋅(Cu)=∇⋅(D∇C).
(50)
For constant D and incompressible flow, this reduces to Ct​+u⋅∇C=D∇2C, where ∇2 is the Laplacian. In a stationary carrier it is the diffusion equation. These assumptions matter: variable D must remain inside the divergence, and changing sources require extra terms. [ref]
The useful surprise is the common mathematics: thermal conduction smooths temperature through the analogous heat equation, while molecular diffusion smooths composition. This analogy already motivated the original formulation of Fick's laws. [ref] However, the thermal diffusivity and the solutal diffusivity need not be equal. A diffusive time scale tD​∼L2/D means that crossing ten times the distance requires roughly one hundred times the time. This is why molecular diffusion is especially effective across thin layers, and why chaotic advection can assist mixing by making those layers thinner. Physical diffusion is a transport mechanism, distinct from the broader probabilistic class of Markov diffusion.

Molecular diffusion

Words: 901
Diffusion OurBigBook.com
Molecular diffusion is the component of material transport caused by the random thermal motion of molecules, measured relative to bulk motion of their surroundings. A diffusion coefficient is a property of a particular substance in a particular medium under specified conditions, not a universal speed of spreading. Its dependence on the solute, solvent and temperature is precisely what makes a spreading experiment informative. A random walk idealizes this motion; the Brownian motion description provides a continuous approximation over sufficiently long times. [ref]
A motivating experiment: watch dye enter a gel. Samprovalaki, Robbins and Fryer studied rhodamine 6G and methylene blue entering agar gel from two side reservoirs. A covered slab, 10×5×1mm, sat on a controlled thermal stage; the dye was brought to the same temperature. They photographed the gel every ten minutes, averaged image intensity across a strip, and fitted the changing concentration to a diffusion equation model. The cover limited evaporation and stopped dye travelling over the gel surface. Runs at 30, 50 and 70∘C were repeated in triplicate. The measured spatial colour change therefore supplied a quantitative transport test, rather than merely showing that dye eventually spreads. Changing lighting also changes image intensity, so the optical response had to be checked. Importantly for interpretation, their constant-diffusion coefficient fit was imperfect and the gel coefficient is an effective transport coefficient, not automatically the value in free water. [ref]
A finite-pulse version to test width growth. The following is a proposed teaching variant, not that paper's apparatus or a report of measurements. Make a long, narrow, transparent gel channel of uniform cross-section. Join a thin dyed gel band between two undyed lengths of the same gel, with good contact and no air gaps; the dye should initially fill the cross-section so the dominant concentration variation is along the channel coordinate x. After assembly, keep the covered channel horizontal at uniform temperature, away from vibration. The dye is a finite initial pulse: no reservoir supplies more dye. Choose a dye whose image response can be calibrated and whose interaction with the gel is small enough for an approximately constant diffusion coefficient to be plausible.
Photograph the whole pulse at recorded times with fixed lighting, focus and exposure, including a length scale. Use uniformly dyed standards of the same gel thickness and a blank gel to convert image intensity to concentration C(x,t); do not assume raw brightness is proportional to concentration. Average across the channel width and examine several parallel strips to check the one-dimensional approximation. Measure the initial profile instead of treating the band as infinitely thin. For a finite pulse with negligible end effects, define its spatial integral Q, centre xˉ and width σ by
Q=∫−∞∞​C(x,t)dx,xˉ(t)=Q1​∫−∞∞​xC(x,t)dx,σ2(t)=Q1​∫−∞∞​(x−xˉ(t))2C(x,t)dx.
(51)
Here σ2 is the variance of the normalized profile C/Q, and σ is its standard deviation. If C is measured in molm−3, then Q has units molm−2; multiplying by the channel cross-section gives the total amount of substance. For the unbounded one-dimensional diffusion equation with constant D, conserved Q, finite variance and sufficiently decaying tails,
σ2(t)=σ02​+2Dt,D=21​dtdσ2​.
(52)
Thus plot width squared against time: its slope determines the diffusion coefficient, while its intercept includes the finite starting width. This moment law holds even for a non-Gaussian distribution initially; it follows by applying integration by parts twice to the diffusion equation. [ref]
For the particularly readable case of an initially Gaussian distribution centred at zero, uniform advection at speed u and constant diffusion coefficient D give the one-dimensional concentration profile
C(x,t)=2π(σ02​+2Dt)​Q​exp[−2(σ02​+2Dt)(x−ut)2​].
(53)
Its centre moves as xˉ=ut and its variance grows as σ02​+2Dt. Our illustrative choice σ0​=0.50mm and D=0.20mm2h−1 gives widths 0.50, 0.81 and 1.36mm at zero, one and four hours. These are calculated values, not a measured dye coefficient. Once 2Dt dominates the initial variance, width grows as 2Dt​: four times the elapsed time gives approximately twice the width. A rectangular starting band will not immediately have a Gaussian distribution, although the same width-squared law still applies under the stated assumptions.
Controls and limits of the interpretation. In the proposed experiment, check that Q stays constant and that the centre remains stationary while the width increases. Include a blank and a uniformly dyed gel photographed over the same period: an apparent signal change there exposes lighting drift, dye fading or evaporation. Repeat with a lower starting dye concentration and a second initial width; agreement of the slopes is a check on constant D and on preparation effects. Keep the pulse far from the channel ends and record its faint tails: truncation and background errors can strongly bias a variance. Poor contact, dye binding, chemical reactions or transport in a liquid film can invalidate the simple model. A gel suppresses bulk liquid motion, but its inferred diffusivity need not equal that in the pure solvent. A stationary centre alone does not exclude symmetric flows, and linear width-squared growth alone does not prove a molecular mechanism: turbulence can also produce an effective diffusive description. These are reasons to combine the profile test with the controlled setup.

Rotational diffusion (Dr​)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Diffusion OurBigBook.com
Rotational diffusion is the random change of a particle's rigid body orientation through Brownian motion. A suspended ellipsoid can turn while its centre hardly moves; translational diffusion instead spreads its position. Random molecular collisions supply fluctuating torques as well as forces. The rotational diffusion coefficient Dr​ measures how quickly angular uncertainty grows, rather than a steady spin speed. Its units are s−1, often written rad2s−1 to distinguish angular spreading from translational spreading, whose diffusion coefficient Dt​ has units m2s−1. The radian is dimensionless, but writing angular variance in rad2 remains useful.
First identify what the image can reveal. A marked end of an elongated particle defines an arrow: turning it through π reverses that arrow. An unmarked ellipsoid with identical ends reveals only its long axis, a director: angles ϕ and ϕ+π describe the same visible state. An unmarked perfect sphere has no visible rigid body orientation at all. Tracking its centre cannot measure its rotational diffusion; a surface mark or another identifiable internal direction is needed.
This distinction makes rotational diffusion useful: it measures how long a particle remembers its pointing direction. For an elongated particle, turning also changes which laboratory direction is easiest for translational diffusion. Randomization of rigid body orientation can therefore erase directional preferences in the observed displacement, even though the particle's shape has not changed.

Planar rotational diffusion (dϕ=2Dr​​dW)

Words: 301
Rotational diffusion OurBigBook.com
For free planar turning with constant Dr​, no imposed torque and negligible inertia, model an unwrapped angle by the stochastic differential equation
dϕ=2Dr​​dW,Δϕ=ϕ(t)−ϕ(0),⟨Δϕ⟩=0,⟨(Δϕ)2⟩=2Dr​t.
(54)
Here W is standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, with increment variance dt, and brackets denote expected values over repeated realizations. The angular variance is conventionally reported in rad2. “Unwrapped” means recording accumulated turns continuously, rather than resetting the angle at each revolution. Directly subtracting wrapped camera angles creates artificial jumps; for an unmarked ellipsoid the wrapping period is π, and resolving successive turns additionally requires sufficiently frequent images.
For a planar arrow u=(cosϕ,sinϕ), the orientational autocorrelation is
Carrow​(t)=⟨u(t)⋅u(0)⟩=⟨cosΔϕ⟩=e−Dr​t.
(55)
For an unoriented planar axis, use an autocorrelation unchanged by replacing either endpoint angle by that angle plus π:
Caxis​(t)=⟨cos(2Δϕ)⟩=e−4Dr​t.
(56)
The same Dr​ thus gives arrow and axis correlation times 1/Dr​ and 1/(4Dr​), respectively, where a correlation time here is the lag at which the relevant curve reaches 1/e. A short explanation is enough: Δϕ has a Gaussian distribution of variance 2Dr​t, so its characteristic function gives ⟨cos(nΔϕ)⟩=e−n2Dr​t. The integer n selects what the observable can distinguish; it does not change the underlying angular spreading.
For an original numerical example, choose Dr​=0.25s−1. After 2s, the angular variance is 1rad2 and its root mean square displacement is 1rad, although the mean displacement is zero. The planar arrow autocorrelation is e−0.5≃0.607, while the planar axis autocorrelation is e−2≃0.135. Calling both “the orientation correlation” without specifying the observable would hide a factor of four in decay rate.

In 2006, Yilong Han and colleagues dispersed plastic ellipsoids in water inside a thin glass cell, using a very dilute suspension to limit particle interactions. A camera on an optical microscope recorded 30 frames per second. Image analysis extracted centre positions and long-axis angles, with reported angular resolution about 1∘. Their shape supplied the observable axis. Reflected interference colours calibrated cell thickness; nearly constant particle interference colour checked vertical wandering. One tracked particle had dimensions 2.4×0.3×0.3μm in an 846nm gap. Angular displacement variance grew linearly with lag; displacement resolved along the particle's axes and in the laboratory showed how turning washes out translational anisotropy. These are observations of confined particles: walls alter drag, and slight out-of-plane tumbling affected positional resolution. They do not establish the bulk sphere formula. The paper's Figure 1A–B shows simulations; Figure 1F shows a measured trajectory.[ref]
For interpreting such images, the director distinction is essential: identical ends give an angle modulo π. A continuously unwrapped trace can follow small successive turns, but it does not make the ends physically distinguishable. The invariant planar axis autocorrelation is ⟨cos(2Δϕ)⟩, and its decay determines Dr​ through e−4Dr​t. Separately measuring position and rigid body orientation is what makes the connection between translational anisotropy and loss of angular memory experimentally accessible.

Thermal expansion is a change in a body's dimensions as its temperature changes under a specified mechanical constraint. A heated gas under a freely moving loaded piston usually increases its volume at fixed pressure; heating the same gas in a rigid vessel instead raises its pressure. The coefficient of thermal expansion quantifies the first response. Expansion can be negative, so the name does not assert that every substance grows on heating.
For an ideal gas at fixed pressure and particle number, V=NkB​T/P gives V2​/V1​=T2​/T1​. Heating from 300K to 330K therefore increases the volume by exactly 10% within the ideal gas model. For a solid, specify whether the measurement concerns length or volume: for uniform expansion in all three directions, the volumetric coefficient is three times the linear thermal expansion coefficient, because V∝L3. Direction-dependent expansion requires the separate dimensional responses. [ref]

Boltzmann distribution (Pi​=Z−1e−βEi​)

Words: 821 Articles: 5
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
The Boltzmann distribution assigns probabilities to individual microstates in a canonical ensemble, a statistical ensemble for thermal contact. The system exchanges energy with a thermal reservoir at fixed positive absolute temperature T, while its particle number N and external parameters, such as volume, stay fixed. The thermal reservoir is large enough that these exchanges barely change its temperature; the coupling permits thermal equilibrium but contributes negligible interaction energy. All the microstates considered have the same N. No chemical potential term is needed in their weights; fixed N does not imply that the chemical potential is zero.
For a finite discrete set of microstates with energies Ei​, write
pi​=Ze−βEi​​,β=kB​T1​,Z=∑i​e−βEi​,∑i​pi​=1.
(64)
Here kB​ is the Boltzmann constant, β is the inverse temperature, e−βEi​ is a Boltzmann factor, and Z is the partition function. The Boltzmann factor is a weight; dividing by the partition function makes it a probability. [ref]
The useful surprise is that a fixed temperature still permits thermal fluctuations in the system's energy. The Boltzmann distribution predicts their probabilities and expected values without tracking every microscopic exchange. Its exponential function also makes rare excited microstates sensitive to temperature: an energy gap much larger than kB​T gives strong Boltzmann suppression, while warming increases their relative populations. A population ratio can therefore reveal a gap or serve as a thermometer, provided thermal equilibrium and the relevant state degeneracies are known.
Historically, Josiah Willard Gibbs's Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902) presents the canonical ensemble in Chapter IV. His equations 90–92 give an exponential function of energy and its normalization, in classical phase space. This classical formulation exhibits the same weighting principle. [ref] [ref]

The expected value of energy rises from zero toward Δ in this finite model.

Low-temperature Gibbs free-energy expansion (G(T,p)=G(0,p)−∫0T​S(t,p)dt)

Words: 55
Third law of thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
At fixed pressure and material content, S=−(∂G/∂T)p​. If the equilibrium entropy tends to zero, the Gibbs free energy approaches its zero-temperature value with zero slope. When Cp​=aTr+o(Tr) with r>0 and zero residual entropy, integrating dS=Cp​dT/T gives S=(a/r)Tr+o(Tr) and G=G(0,p)−aTr+1/[r(r+1)]+o(Tr+1). Nonzero residual entropy S0​ instead contributes −S0​T to G; a horizontal limiting tangent requires the zero-entropy hypothesis.

Unattainability of absolute zero

Words: 97
Third law of thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
In a regular thermodynamic formulation, a state at absolute zero cannot be reached from positive temperature by finitely many cooling operations with finite control resources. The entropy-difference form of the third law of thermodynamics makes regular entropy curves approach a common limiting entropy. An isentropic process starting above that entropy cannot intersect the common zero-temperature endpoint.
For an illustrative pair of settings with S−S0​=a1​T and S−S0​=a2​T, 0<a1​<a2​, an isothermal entropy-reduction step followed by reversible adiabatic cooling gives Tn+1​=(a1​/a2​)Tn​. Every finite number of stages leaves Tn​>0. The model illustrates the entropy geometry; a general finite-time impossibility statement additionally needs assumptions about available interactions and cooling rates.

Intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
An extensive quantity measures how much of a thermodynamic system there is; an intensive quantity describes its state independently of that amount. The clean comparison is replication: take independent identical systems at the same thermodynamic equilibrium, with the same substance, composition and thermodynamic phase. Combining their accounting boundaries multiplies internal energy U, entropy S, volume V, mass m and amount of substance n, while leaving temperature T, pressure p and chemical potential μ unchanged.[ref]
For λ copies the ledger is
(U,S,V,m,n)⟼λ(U,S,V,m,n),(T,p,μ)⟼(T,p,μ).
(74)
An integer λ counts actual copies; a positive real λ describes the corresponding bulk scaling law. Copies can remain separated: replication need not involve removing a partition, changing a container or performing any work. Distinguish n, the amount of substance measured in moles, from N=nNA​, the dimensionless count of specified entities, where NA​ is the Avogadro constant in mol−1. For example, 2mol contains 1.204428152×1024 specified entities; tripling it gives 6mol and 3.613284456×1024 entities. This uses the exact Avogadro constant NA​=6.02214076×1023mol−1, which does not triple. In the differential dU=TdS−pdV+μdn, μ is a molar chemical potential in Jmol−1; the coefficient of dN instead has units of energy per entity.
As a direct check, the ideal gas law pV=nRT gives
p′=λV(λn)RT​=p.
(75)
For a monatomic ideal gas with only translational degrees of freedom active, internal energy of an ideal gas gives U=3nRT/2, so U′=λU at unchanged temperature. Here R is the molar gas constant. The scaling distinction lets a small sample supply an equation of state for a much larger amount: material state and inventory become separate questions.
Replication does not mean multiplying every linear dimension by λ: a geometrically similar container then has λ3 times the volume. Nor does it mean combining samples at different states. Equal temperature establishes thermal equilibrium but does not imply equal pressure, composition or mass density. Density of a composite system makes this distinction concrete.

Extensive quantity

Words: 298 Articles: 1
Intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities OurBigBook.com
Two related properties of an extensive quantity must be distinguished. Additivity says that a quantity X for independent subsystems A and B obeys
XA∪B​=XA​+XB​.
(76)
The subsystems may be in different states. Extensivity expressed through a homogeneous function says that the equilibrium fundamental relation obeys
U(λS,λV,λn)=λU(S,V,n),λ>0,
(77)
with composition held fixed. This is degree-one homogeneity along a replication ray; it does not say that internal energy is a linear function of arbitrary independent changes of entropy, volume and amount of substance.
Additivity gives integer replication by repeated addition. Subdividing a uniform bulk sample into b equivalent parts gives rational scaling a/b; continuity then extends it to positive real factors. This argument requires negligible boundary contributions and a consistently prepared state. Conversely, a degree-one homogeneous function need not be additive between different rays: f(x,y)=x2+y2​ has f(λx,λy)=λf(x,y), but f(1,0)+f(0,1)=2=2​=f(1,1). Thus a scaling identity alone cannot justify summing arbitrary states.
For finite samples, the surface correction to thermodynamic free energy can matter. Under geometric enlargement with volume multiplied by λ, surface area grows as λ2/3, so a surface energy term is not a bulk extensive quantity. Replicating separated droplets retains every original surface, whereas merging them changes the total surface area. Likewise, appreciable mutual gravitational potential energy makes interacting subsystems fail the independent-copy premise. The thermodynamic limit explains when bulk scaling becomes accurate; it does not remove these qualifications for every small or strongly interacting system.

Euler relation in thermodynamics (E=TS−PV+μN)

Words: 85
Extensive quantity OurBigBook.com
For a single-component equilibrium system with extensive internal energy E(S,V,N), scaling its entropy, volume and particle number together gives E(λS,λV,λN)=λE(S,V,N). The Euler theorem for homogeneous functions therefore gives E=S∂S​E+V∂V​E+N∂N​E. The first law of thermodynamics identifies these derivatives as T,−P,μ, respectively, proving E=TS−PV+μN. Dividing by volume yields the entropy density formula s=(ρ+P−μn)/T. This step fixes the entropy normalization rather than merely identifying its differential. Differentiating the Euler relation and subtracting dE=TdS−PdV+μdN gives the Gibbs-Duhem equation SdT−VdP+Ndμ=0. The argument requires extensivity; it is not an assumption about arbitrary nonadditive systems.

Intensive quantity

Words: 805 Articles: 3
Intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities OurBigBook.com
An intensive quantity is unchanged under replication at the same thermodynamic equilibrium. Temperature, pressure, chemical potential and the mass density of a uniform substance are examples. Independence from sample size does not mean independence from state: a material's mass density can change with temperature or pressure.
The relation to extensive quantities is particularly elegant for a differentiable bulk fundamental relation. Put x=(S,V,n) and write
U(λx)=λU(x).
(78)
Taking a partial derivative with respect to xi​ and cancelling λ gives
∂xi​∂U​(λx)=∂xi​∂U​(x).
(79)
The equilibrium differential dU=TdS−pdV+μdn identifies these derivatives with temperature, minus pressure and molar chemical potential. They are degree-zero homogeneous functions. The same degree-one assumption yields the Euler relation in thermodynamics, but a surface energy contribution requires extra care.
An intensive quantity generally has no meaningful sum across samples: two equal temperatures do not add to a doubled temperature. Neither is the final temperature after thermal contact generally an unweighted average; heat capacities and the first law of thermodynamics determine the balance. Ratios of additive inventories lead to the useful weighted rules in normalizing extensive quantities.

Normalizing extensive quantities

Words: 655 Articles: 2
Intensive quantity OurBigBook.com
Dividing two extensive quantities with the same replication factor produces an intensive quantity:
λYλX​=YX​,Y>0.
(80)
Division by volume gives a density, such as mass density ρ=m/V or energy density U/V. Division by mass gives a specific quantity, such as specific internal energy u=U/m or specific volume v=V/m. Division by amount of substance gives a molar quantity, such as molar volume Vm​=V/n. Their units are respectively kgm−3, Jm−3, Jkg−1, m3kg−1 and m3mol−1. The denominator must be stated: “per particle”, “per mole” and “per unit mass” are different normalizations.
For a hypothetical uniform parcel with mass 2kg, volume 0.002m3 and internal energy 40kJ relative to a specified reference, u=20kJkg−1 and ρ=1000kgm−3. Three independent copies have 6kg, 0.006m3 and 120kJ; both ratios remain unchanged. This permits comparison of materials without confusing the amount tested with the state tested.
If X and Y are additive but the parcels have different ri​=Xi​/Yi​, their composite ratio is a weighted arithmetic mean:
rtotal​=∑i​Yi​∑i​Xi​​=∑i​∑j​Yj​Yi​​ri​.
(81)
The denominator supplies the weights: specific internal energy uses mass weights, while mass density uses volume weights. This identity is accounting for the specified subsystems; predicting a new state after mixing also needs the relevant equation of state.
Density of a composite system (ρtotal​=(mA​+mB​)/(VA​+VB​))
Words: 198
Normalizing extensive quantities OurBigBook.com
Consider two hypothetical parcels at the same temperature 300K, kept separated with negligible partition mass and excluded container volume. Parcel A has mass 2kg and volume 0.002m3; parcel B has mass 3kg and volume 0.006m3. They may be different materials. Their individual mass densities and the composite mass density are
ρA​=1000kgm−3,ρB​=500kgm−3,ρtotal​=0.008m35kg​=625kgm−3.
(82)
The composite mass density is total material mass divided by total occupied volume; it need not be the local mass density anywhere. Equal temperature does not make these parcels replicas. In particular, the unweighted average 750kgm−3 is wrong. The volume fractions are 1/4 and 3/4, giving
ρtotal​=41​ρA​+43​ρB​=625kgm−3.
(83)
With mass fractions 2/5 and 3/5, the equivalent rule is a weighted harmonic mean:
ρtotal​1​=ρA​2/5​+ρB​3/5​=0.0016m3kg−1.
(84)
This follows directly by writing Vi​=mi​/ρi​ and dividing total volume by total mass; it is also the mass-weighted average of specific volumes. An unweighted average of mass densities is valid when the parcel volume values are equal, not merely when their temperatures are equal.
If a partition is removed and different substances mix, the final volume need not equal the sum of initial volume values. A new temperature, thermodynamic phase or composition may also change the local mass density. Use the actual final volume in ρ=m/V; the pre-mixing weighted identity cannot supply it. Even unchanged temperature alone does not guarantee unchanged volume.
Pycnometer density measurement
Words: 266
Normalizing extensive quantities OurBigBook.com
A pycnometer makes the distinction between mass and mass density experimentally tangible. NIST's 1994 report describes a glass vessel with filling capillaries, wire plugs and a covered overflow bowl in a controlled water bath. The operators soaked a pure-water filling to establish the bath temperature, dried the outside, then left it overnight in the balance enclosure to reach thermal equilibrium before weighing. Empty and full force-restoration balance readings, together with known water mass density, calibrated its capacity at the bath temperature. A tin-oxide coating suppressed stray electric charge; an electrometer detected none during use. The authors distinguish bath and weighing temperatures and correct for buoyancy and changes of displacement volume. Capacity and water-reference uncertainties carry into later liquid mass density determinations. Their pycnometer data were not yet analyzed, so this account provides no measured density or achieved precision.[ref]
The ideal accounting behind this measurement calibration can be derived without numerical observations. Let m0​,mw​,mx​ denote corrected masses of the empty vessel, water-filled vessel and sample-filled vessel. At the same filling temperature, with known reference water mass density ρw​ and reproducibly filled volume Vc​,
Vc​=ρw​mw​−m0​​,ρx​=Vc​mx​−m0​​=ρw​mw​−m0​mx​−m0​​.
(85)
The empty-vessel subtraction removes vessel mass; the water filling sets volume. Doubling Vc​ for the same uniform sample doubles the sample mass increment but preserves ρx​. Uncorrected balance indications, trapped bubbles, incomplete filling or unequal filling temperatures break the simple identification with corrected mass and a common Vc​. This explains why replication is a statement about comparable states rather than arbitrary instrument readings.

Gibbs-Duhem equation (SdT−Vdp+∑i​ni​dμi​=0)

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
The Euler theorem for homogeneous functions applied to an extensive quantity, together with dE=TdS−pdV+μdN give
E=TS−pV+μN,SdT−Vdp+Ndμ=0.
(86)
The Gibbs-Duhem equation constrains changes of the intensive quantities describing one uniform thermodynamic phase. For a mixture with k independently specified component amounts, its molar form is
SdT−Vdp+∑i=1k​ni​dμi​=0.
(87)
Here S is entropy, V is volume, T is temperature, p is pressure, ni​ is the amount of substance of component i, and μi​ is its molar chemical potential. This assumes a simple compressible system whose bulk internal energy is an extensive quantity; additional work coordinates require additional terms.[ref]
The proof exposes the source of the constraint. For internal energy E(S,V,n1​,…,nk​), replication of the whole thermodynamic phase by a factor λ gives E(λS,λV,λn1​,…,λnk​)=λE(S,V,n1​,…,nk​). The Euler theorem for homogeneous functions and the fundamental differential of internal energy therefore give
E=TS−pV+∑i​μi​ni​,dE=TdS−pdV+∑i​μi​dni​.
(88)
Taking the differential of the first equation produces all the terms in the second, plus SdT−Vdp+∑i​ni​dμi​. Subtraction proves the Gibbs-Duhem equation. Thus the constraint comes from two descriptions of the same state function, rather than an assumed microscopic interaction model.
At fixed temperature and pressure, divide by n=∑i​ni​>0 and introduce the mole fractions xi​=ni​/n:
∑i​xi​dμi​=0.
(89)
The chemical potentials cannot be varied independently. In a two-component mixture, put xA​=x and xB​=1−x. Within a smooth single-thermodynamic phase region with 0<x<1,
x(∂x∂μA​​)T,p​+(1−x)(∂x∂μB​​)T,p​=0,dμB​=−1−xx​dμA​.
(90)
One chemical potential fixes the other's change, but determining its absolute value still requires a reference value. This does not say μA​=μB​: equality at phase coexistence concerns the same chemical species in different thermodynamic phases. Nor does the constraint say dG=0 whenever temperature and pressure are fixed; changing composition still contributes ∑i​μi​dni​ to the Gibbs free energy.

Ideal binary Gibbs-Duhem cancellation (xdμA​+(1−x)dμB​=0)

Words: 288
Gibbs-Duhem equation OurBigBook.com
An ideal solution has molar chemical potentials
μA​=μA∗​(T,p)+RTlnx,μB​=μB∗​(T,p)+RTln(1−x),
(91)
where R is the molar gas constant and the stars denote pure-component reference values at the same temperature and pressure.[ref]
Hold temperature and pressure fixed. The derivatives with respect to x are RT/x and −RT/(1−x), so
xdxdμA​​=RT,(1−x)dxdμB​​=−RT.
(92)
Each chemical potential changes, yet their composition-weighted slopes cancel exactly. At x=1/4, the two slopes are 4RT and −4RT/3; multiplying by 1/4 and 3/4 gives RT and −RT. Near either pure-component endpoint the dilute component's slope diverges, but its weighted contribution remains finite. The endpoint chemical potential itself requires a limiting interpretation because its logarithm diverges.
The same constraint has a geometric explanation. Subtract the pure-component reference contribution from the molar Gibbs free energy and divide by RT to obtain
f(x)=xlnx+(1−x)ln(1−x).
(93)
Its derivative is f′(x)=ln[x/(1−x)]. At fixed total amount of substance, exchanging a little B for A changes the Gibbs free energy with slope μA​−μB​. Consequently the tangent to f at x has intercepts
f(x)−xf′(x)=ln(1−x),f(x)+(1−x)f′(x)=lnx
(94)
at horizontal coordinates 0 and 1, respectively. The two chemical potentials come from the same curve: choosing two unrelated functions would generally destroy this tangent construction.

Binary activity-coefficient consistency (xdlnγA​+(1−x)dlnγB​=0)

Words: 238
Gibbs-Duhem equation OurBigBook.com
For a nonideal chemical solution, write its thermodynamic activities on a mole fraction basis as aA​=xγA​ and aB​=(1−x)γB​. Use composition-independent pure-component reference chemical potentials at the same temperature and pressure:
μA​=μA∗​+RTln(xγA​),μB​=μB∗​+RTln[(1−x)γB​].
(95)
The activity coefficients describe departure from the ideal solution under that reference convention.[ref]
At fixed temperature and pressure, insert these expressions into the Gibbs-Duhem equation. The ideal solution terms cancel because xdlnx+(1−x)dln(1−x)=dx−dx=0. What remains is
xdlnγA​+(1−x)dlnγB​=0.
(96)
Thus two independent fits to measured activity coefficients can each look smooth while failing to describe one possible Gibbs free energy. This is a necessary consistency condition; satisfying it alone does not establish experimental accuracy or thermodynamic stability.
For an original algebraic example, suppose at one fixed temperature and pressure that lnγA​=α(1−x)2, with dimensionless constant α. The constraint requires dlnγB​/dx=2αx. With the pure-B normalization γB​(0)=1, integration gives
lnγB​=αx2.
(97)
For α=1/2 and x=1/4, the derivatives of the two logarithms are −3/4 and 1/4; their weighted sum is −3/16+3/16=0. Choosing lnγB​=αx instead would give a weighted sum 3/16 at that composition, contradicting the Gibbs-Duhem equation. These are invented model functions, with no claim to fit a particular mixture.
The fixed-temperature, fixed-pressure restriction matters. Along a path with changing temperature or pressure, the general equation contains SdT−Vdp, and the reference chemical potentials and RT also change. Across phase coexistence, apply the relation separately within each smooth thermodynamic phase; do not differentiate a discontinuous switch between phases as if it were a single composition curve.

Mixture measurements and the Gibbs-Duhem constraint

Words: 316
Gibbs-Duhem equation OurBigBook.com
A concrete motivating experiment is the acetone–chloroform mixture in Truman State University's Liquid-Vapor Equilibrium of a Binary System, Procedure and Figure 1. A two-neck flask feeds a distillation head with a water-cooled laboratory condenser, condensate sampling arm and temperature probe. Starting with one pure liquid, the procedure adds the other component successively and waits for stable temperature with returning condensate. Small paired samples from the flask and condensate are read on an Abbé refractometer; a tabulated refractive index–composition relation gives the two compositions. Controls include three-point thermometer calibration, corrected atmospheric pressure readings, and agreement of the initial pure-liquid and condensate refractive indices with the reference value. Small withdrawals and little retained condensate reduce disturbance of composition. Sample evaporation can bias the readout. The inferred paired mole fractions, temperature and pressure describe vapor-liquid equilibrium, subject to the conversion from mass fraction to mole fraction and to representative sampling. This teaching protocol reports no measured results of a particular student run.[ref]
How does such a measurement expose activity coefficients? Let xi​ and yi​ be the mole fractions in the liquid and gas thermodynamic phases, respectively, and let pi∗​(T) be the pure-component vapor pressure. Assume the gas thermodynamic phase is an ideal gas mixture and neglect the change of the pure-liquid reference chemical potential between its saturation pressure and the experimental pressure. Equality of each component's chemical potential between the two thermodynamic phases then gives
RTln(xi​γi​)=RTlnpi∗​(T)yi​p​,γi​≃xi​pi∗​(T)yi​p​.
(98)
This turns the paired composition readings into estimates of the activity coefficients. The approximation needs refinement when the gas departs appreciably from ideal gas behavior or the neglected liquid pressure effect matters.
The apparatus measures a boiling-composition series in which temperature changes as the mixture changes. Its readings therefore cannot be inserted directly into the fixed-temperature, fixed-pressure activity coefficient constraint. They motivate the more general task: test whether the measured mixture properties can arise from a common Gibbs free energy while accounting for changing state variables. A failure can reveal incompatible property fits or experimental bias; a pass supplies a consistency check, not proof that every reading is correct.

Thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A thermodynamic cycle returns a working substance to its initial state. Its net internal-energy change is zero, so the net work output equals net heat input.

Atkinson cycle

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Thermodynamic cycle OurBigBook.com
The ideal Atkinson cycle considered here has reversible adiabatic compression, isochoric heat addition, a longer reversible adiabatic expansion and isobaric heat rejection. Its expansion ends at the initial pressure rather than at the initial volume. With constant ideal-gas heat capacities, r=V1​/V2​ and rp​=p3​/p2​, the temperatures are T2​=T1​rγ−1, T3​=rp​T2​, and T4′​=T1​rp1/γ​. This ideal cycle is distinguished from the detailed valve timing and losses of a practical engine.

Atkinson efficiency advantage from extended expansion (ηA​=1−γr1−γ(rp1/γ​−1)/(rp​−1))

Words: 68
Atkinson cycle OurBigBook.com
For the same initial state, compression ratio and constant-volume heat input, the ideal Atkinson cycle adds net work during the extended expansion and subsequent constant-pressure return. The extra work is the integral of pexpansion​−p1​ over the added volume, which is positive. Equivalently, concavity of x1/γ gives γ(rp1/γ​−1)<rp​−1 when rp​>1 and γ>1, so its efficiency exceeds the corresponding Otto cycle efficiency. The comparison fixes these shared conditions rather than asserting universal superiority under arbitrary engine constraints.

Brayton cycle

Words: 128 Articles: 1
Thermodynamic cycle OurBigBook.com
The ideal Brayton cycle consists of adiabatic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, adiabatic expansion, and constant-pressure heat rejection. Its ideal working substance is an ideal gas with constant heat capacities, and the insulated stages are reversible thermodynamic processes.
For pressure ratio rp​=ph​/pl​ and heat capacity ratio γ=Cp​/CV​, a reversible ideal-gas adiabat has T∝p(γ−1)/γ. Thus T2​/T1​=T3​/T4​=k=rp(γ−1)/γ​, and the constant-pressure heat transfers have Qout​/Qin​=(T4​−T1​)/(T3​−T2​)=1/k. The thermal efficiency is
η=1−rp−(γ−1)/γ​.​
(99)
This formula requires constant heat capacities and internally reversible insulated stages. An arbitrary dissipative adiabatic process does not satisfy the same pressure-temperature relation.

Brayton-Carnot efficiency comparison (ηC​−ηB​=r−1(1−TA​/TB​)>0)

Words: 52
Brayton cycle OurBigBook.com
For constant-pressure heat addition A→B and two reversible ideal-gas adiabats, set r=(ph​/pl​)(γ−1)/γ. The Brayton cycle has ηB​=1−1/r, maximum temperature TB​ and minimum TD​=TA​/r. A Carnot cycle using those extreme temperatures has the strictly greater efficiency displayed whenever TB​>TA​. Reversibility of the isobaric heating requires continuously matched reservoir temperatures, rather than heat transfer solely at the maximum temperature.

Vanishing-cutoff limit of the Diesel cycle (η→1−r1−γ)

Words: 76
Diesel cycle OurBigBook.com
For an ideal Diesel cycle with compression ratio r=V1​/V2​>1, cutoff ratio ρ=V3​/V2​>1 and constant heat-capacity ratio γ, its thermal efficiency is η=1−(ργ−1)/[γrγ−1(ρ−1)]. As ρ→1+ the quotient tends to γ, giving η→1−r1−γ. The maximum-to-minimum temperature ratio tends to rγ−1, so the limiting efficiency equals that of a Carnot cycle between those temperatures. Both heat input and net work vanish in this limit: the result is a limit of their ratio, not a finite-work engine at exactly zero cutoff interval.
